newsitem.title: FRANCE: French cap market pain less if Socialists dominate.
newsitem.headline: French cap market pain less if Socialists dominate.

text.p: French interest rate and bond futures were seen opening slightly lower on Monday after a first round runoff vote in a parliamentary election pointed to a victory for the left, analysts said.

But they said there would not be much damage if the Socialists scored an outright victory because the policy outlook would be more uncertain if they had to rely on support from the Communists, who want a referendum on whether to go ahead with a single European currency.

"It looks like the Socialists have an absolute majority so the market reaction may be rather soft," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance said. "I would still say slightly negative but maybe not all that much."
He said he expected the difference between French and German 10-year bond yields to narrow slightly from minus 15 basis points before the first projections were released at 1800 GMT.

Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris, said, "What is interesting is that the Socialists could have majority alone which is not so bad for markets. They would be less prone to be influenced by the Communists on both economic and European policies."

Nevertheless, analysts said even with an absolute majority for the Socialists, there were additional risks that the move towards monetary union would not be as smooth as it would have been if the centre-right coalition had retained power.

"From a market point of view it's probably a second best result, the worst result was going to be a hung parliament. But the ultimate left-right debate is the same one," Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais, said.

"One has to assume that the government will not be nearly as aggressive in terms of managing the public sector, which means running a higher risk of slippage going forward, a risk of an overshoot of the Maastricht critieria and a risk of uncomfortable political tension between France and Germany," Lindsay said.
"The (market) direction has to be on the weakening side and PIBOR will clearly have to lead. I think it's mildly supportive that it's the Socialist party alone but it's fairly second order," he said.
Maire Owens Thomsen said an absolute majority for the Socialists would probably limit the fallout in the bond market.

"The 10-year Oat-Bund spread should not go into positive territory if the Socialists form a governmnt on their own," she said. "Our worst case scenario was for the spread to go to plus 20. There is a fair chance with these results that it won't turn positive."
Dominique Barbet, economist at Banque Paribas, also said while French markets would probably fall the damage would be limited if the Socialists won an absolute majority.

"I think the market reaction will obviously not be positive but the victory is clear and the fall in markets should be relatively limited, especially if the Socialists absolute majority alone is confirmed.
It (the fall) will perhaps be a bit stronger on the stock market than on PIBOR (interest rate futures).

June PIBOR has come under the most pressure since talk of an early election first hit market prices on April 17. It fell as low as 96.12 in electronic trading last Monday after the left polled a surprise victory in the first round of voting.

However it rallied as high as 96.37 on Friday as many investors bought back contracts they had sold earlier, either because they thought there could be a shock right win or because an outright win for the Socialists might not be that negative.
The bond future also climbed on Friday ahead of the final round of voting to settle at 128.52 for similar reasons.
Trading in French bond and interest rate futures kicks off at 0500 GMT on Monday morning.
